cards.title: Addressing Brazilian Air Force
cards.body: Brazilian Air Force ranks are similar to the US. Use 'senhor' (sir) or 'senhora' (ma'am) with their rank. Civilians use 'senhor' or 'senhora' without rank. Avoid informal language like 'você' (you) with seniors.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Criticism and Disagreement
cards.body: Brazilians value harmony. Criticize privately, indirectly, and gently. Disagree politely, using 'eu acho que' (I think) to soften. Avoid public confrontation or blunt 'no'.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilian culture values hierarchy. Address seniors with formal titles and last names. They appreciate politeness and respect. Use 'senhor' (Mr.) or 'senhora' (Mrs.) followed by their last name.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints in Brazil
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Security staff may ask questions. Locals might be present. Always carry identification. Be patient and cooperative.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Hierarchy in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians value hierarchy and formalities. Use professional titles or 'Senhor/Senhora' with last names for seniors. Avoid direct disagreement with superiors to maintain harmony.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names with seniors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Refusal and Face
cards.body: Brazilians often avoid direct refusal to save face. Use indirect language and offer alternatives. Public criticism is frowned upon; address issues privately.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians value hierarchy and formal titles. Use professional titles like 'Doutor(a)' or 'Senhor/Senhora' with last names in formal settings. For elders or high-ranking individuals, use 'Dom/Seu' or 'Dona'.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names for seniors
Address elders with honorifics like 'Dom/Seu' or 'Dona'

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Save Face in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians avoid direct conflict and value indirect communication. Be diplomatic, avoid public criticism, and use gentle language when disagreeing. Humor is appreciated in casual settings but not in serious discussions.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians value formality and rank in professional settings. Address seniors with their title and last name, e.g., 'Coronel Silva'. Wait for seniors to initiate handshakes. Maintain professionalism to save face.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names
Wait for seniors to initiate physical contact

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigate Brazilian Checkpoints
cards.body: Security staff at base checkpoints may be strict. Have your ID ready. Local nationals may not enter without permission. Be polite and patient to save face.
doThis: Carry your ID at all times
Be patient and polite with security staff

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Addressing Seniors in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilian culture values hierarchy. Always address seniors by their rank and last name initially. Use first names only if invited. Women in authority should be treated with respect, as they may face additional challenges.
doThis: Use formal titles and last names initially
Wait for permission to use first names
avoidThis: Interrupt or disagree openly with seniors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Sensitive Communication in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians value saving face. Criticism should be given privately and constructively. Disagreements should be handled diplomatically to maintain harmony. Refusals may be indirect to avoid causing offense.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respect Religious Hierarchy
cards.body: Brazilian religious leaders, especially in Catholicism, hold significant influence. Show respect to clergy and seniors, as they are highly regarded. Avoid public criticism of religious beliefs or practices.
doThis: Address religious leaders with their titles (e.g., Padre, Pastor).
Show deference to seniors in religious settings.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigate Religious Diversity
cards.body: Brazil has a mix of religions, including Catholicism, evangelical Christianity, Afro-Brazilian religions, and others. Be mindful of religious differences and avoid assumptions. Respect local customs and practices.
doThis: Ask about religious practices before participating.
Respect places of worship and religious events.
avoidThis: Impose your religious beliefs on others.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Gift Giving: Hierarchy and Respect
cards.body: In Brazil, respect for hierarchy is important. When giving gifts, consider the recipient's rank. Gifts are usually given privately and opened later. Avoid giving overly personal or expensive gifts to superiors.
avoidThis: Open gifts in front of the giver

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Gift Refusal: Saving Face
cards.body: Brazilians may refuse gifts to avoid appearing indebted. They might initially decline to save face. If this happens, politely insist once or twice. If they still refuse, respect their decision.
doThis: Respect their decision if they refuse

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Lunch with Brazilian Air Force
cards.body: Lunch is the main meal (early afternoon), often social. Wait to be seated and served. Compliment the food. Decline seconds politely. Eat slowly, enjoy conversation. Use cutlery, not hands.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Dining with Local Civilians
cards.body: Dinner is smaller, served late (7-8pm). Use cutlery. Try everything offered. Conversation is key. If invited, arrive late, bring a gift. Decline politely if full.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respect Hierarchy in Meetings
cards.body: Brazilians value formality and hierarchy in professional settings. Address seniors with their rank and last name. Save face by avoiding public criticism or disagreement. Use indirect language when refusing.
doThis: Address seniors with their rank and last name
avoidThis: Publicly criticizing or disagreeing with seniors

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints and Radio Etiquette
cards.body: Checkpoints and security staff are common on bases. Brazilians may use the 'jeitinho' to bend rules. On the radio, be clear and concise. Avoid discussing flexible rules or implying they are.
doThis: Be clear and concise on the radio

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Respecting Rank in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians value hierarchy. Use formal titles like 'Doutor(a)' or 'Senhor(a)' with last names. For elders or high-ranking officials, use 'Dom', 'Dona', or 'Seu'. Address seniors with respect and deference.
doThis: Use formal titles when addressing seniors.
Show respect and deference to elders and high-ranking officials.
avoidThis: Disrespect hierarchy or chain of command.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Radio Etiquette in Brazil
cards.body: Brazilians appreciate clear, polite communication. Speak slowly and distinctly. Use 'por favor' (please) and 'obrigado(a)' (thank you). Avoid interrupting or speaking over others. Maintain professionalism.
doThis: Use polite phrases like 'por favor' and 'obrigado(a)'.
avoidThis: Use slang or informal language on official channels.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Addressing Brazilian Superiors
cards.body: Brazilian military hierarchy is strict. Use formal titles and last names. Civilians are addressed with titles like 'Doutor' or 'Senhor'. Be respectful and patient, as decisions may take time.
doThis: Use 'Coronel', 'Tenente', etc., with last names for military.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)

cards.title: Navigating Checkpoints and Security
cards.body: Checkpoints are common. Carry ID at all times. Be polite and cooperative with security staff. Locals may be curious; engage politely but keep conversations brief.
doThis: Be polite and cooperative with security.
avoidThis: Be impatient or rude with curiosity.

source.doc: AFCLC Expeditionary Culture Field Guide: Brazil (2025)
